What it does

Binary search on the answer's value range
How many entries are ≤ v, found by a staircase walk from the bottom-left corner in O(n)
In column c everything at or above row r is ≤ v (columns are sorted), so add r+1 entries and move right
matrix[r][c] > v, so the cell and everything below it in this column are too large; move up
mid could be the answer, so keep it
Find the first value with count ≥ k
The smallest value v with count(v) ≥ k, which is guaranteed to be an entry of the matrix

blocks.h: Why is the final `lo` guaranteed to be in the matrix?
p: `lo` ends as the smallest v with count(v) ≥ k. If v were not an entry, count(v−1) would equal count(v) (nothing equals v), contradicting minimality. So v is an entry, and it is exactly the k-th smallest.

bullets: Time: O(n · log(max − min)): each count is O(n) and the range is halved each time.
Space: O(1). A heap approach is O(k log n) and uses O(n) space.

378.takeaway: Binary search on the value range; count(v) is a staircase walk that counts entries ≤ v in O(n).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Private copy of the original for `reset`; `[:]` makes a shallow copy so later swaps do not touch it
Returns a copy so callers cannot mutate internal state
Fisher–Yates: fix positions from the end backwards
Inclusive on both ends: picks any index from 0 to i, including i itself (no change)
Uniform pick among the still-unfixed positions
Places the chosen element in its final position i

p: `[1,2,3]` with a sample random sequence (seeded so it is reproducible; any choices are possible):

At step i there are i + 1 candidates for position i, each chosen with probability 1/(i+1). Multiplying across steps gives 1/(n·(n−1)·…·2) = 1/n! for every permutation, so all n! = 6 orderings of 3 elements have equal probability. Picking j from `0..n−1` at every step would give n^n equally likely paths, which cannot divide evenly into n! outcomes, so it is biased.

bullets: Space: O(n) for the stored original and working copy.

384.takeaway: Fisher–Yates: walk backwards and swap each position with a random earlier-or-same index.

Counts are only final after the whole string has been read: `e` appears at index 1 but occurs three times in total. The second pass walks the string in its original order, so the first character whose final count is 1 is the answer. Each equation adds both directions: a/b = v implies b/a = 1/v

A product of ratios along a path equals x / y
x not in g or y not in g

p: `a/b = 2`, `b/c = 3`. The first two rows are the query `a / c` (the DFS goes a → b → c, and the ratios multiply on the way back); the last two rows are `c / a`:
bullets: Answers: `a/c = 6.0`, `c/a = 0.1667` (path c → b → a with weights 1/3 and 1/2).

blocks.h: Why check `x not in g` before `x == y`?

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Stack of kept digits, non-decreasing from bottom to top (monotonic stack)
A bigger digit just before a smaller one should be removed: the earlier position matters more
Removes as many bigger previous digits as allowed
If removals remain (digits already increasing), drop from the end
Strips leading zeros; the empty result becomes '0'

bullets: k is 0, so nothing more is cut: `1219`.

blocks.h: Why remove a larger digit when a smaller one arrives?
p: Comparing two numbers goes digit by digit from the left, so the leftmost differences matter most. If `st[-1] > d`, deleting `st[-1]` puts a smaller digit in that position and makes the number smaller no matter what follows. The stack therefore only keeps digits that cannot be improved yet.

bullets: Time: O(n), each digit pushed and popped at most once.

p: Leading zeros appear when a `0` becomes the first kept digit (`"10200"`, k=1 gives `"200"`), hence `lstrip('0')`; and `or '0'` covers the case where everything is removed.

402.takeaway: Monotonic stack: pop larger digits when a smaller one arrives, trim leftover removals from the end, strip leading zeros.

p: Without the mask, `-1 >> 4` stays −1 forever in Python and the loop never ends. Masking to 0xFFFFFFFF turns −1 into 4294967295 = `ffffffff`, which matches the two's-complement output the problem expects.

405.takeaway: Hex conversion by peeling 4 bits at a time; mask to 32 bits so negative numbers use two's complement.

p: Input values can themselves be very small (down to −2³¹); a sentinel like −inf would be safe in Python, but `None` makes the empty-slot state explicit and also makes `x in top` safe: a real value never equals `None`. Space: O(1). Sorting a set is O(n log n), and a heap of size 3 is O(n log 3).

What it does
Reach for it when
rows: DFS from all starting cells, moving to neighbours with height ≥ current, i.e. UPHILL, the reverse of how water flows
Sources are seeded at once, so all of them are explored in one search
Reverse flow rule: water can run from (a,b) down to (r,c) if (a,b) is at least as high
Set intersection: cells reachable from both oceans
Converts tuples to lists and orders the output deterministically

p: For the 5×5 grid `[[1, 2, 2, 3, 5], [3, 2, 3, 4, 4], [2, 4, 5, 3, 1], [6, 7, 1, 4, 5], [5, 1, 1, 2, 4]]`, the two floods mark: `P` reaches only the Pacific, `A` only the Atlantic, `B` both:

blocks.h: Why search from the oceans instead of from every cell?
p: Starting a search from each of the m·n cells would cost O(m²n²) in the worst case. Starting from the border cells and walking uphill finds every cell that can reach that ocean in a single O(mn) sweep per ocean, and the intersection gives the cells that reach both.

bullets: Time: O(m·n): every cell is visited at most once per flood.
Space: O(m·n) for the seen sets and stack.

417.takeaway: Reverse the problem: flood uphill from each ocean's border and intersect the two reachable sets.

What it does
Reach for it when

Lets the nested function assign the outer variables `first` (smallest node) and `last` (previously visited node)
Links the previous node and the current node in both directions, reusing the tree's pointers (`left` = prev, `right` = next)
Closes the list into a circle

p: BST `[4,2,5,1,3]`; inorder visits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5:
bullets: Finally `1.left = 5` and `5.right = 1` close the circle; the function returns node 1.

blocks.h: Why does linking during the traversal work?
p: When a node is visited, every smaller node has already been visited and linked into `last`'s chain, and the node's own `left` subtree is no longer needed because it was already traversed. Overwriting `node.left` therefore does not damage the traversal. `node.right` is overwritten only later, when the next node is visited, after `dfs(node.right)` has run on the original right pointer.

bullets: Space: O(h) recursion; no new nodes are created.

426.takeaway: Inorder traversal with a `last` pointer: link each node to the previously visited one, then close the circle.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Sorts by END time (in place); `key` supplies the sort value
End of the last kept interval; nothing kept yet
Starts at or after the last kept end: no overlap (touching is allowed)
Overlaps the kept interval, so drop the current one

blocks.h: Why sort by end and not by start?
p: Keeping the interval that finishes earliest leaves the most room for later ones, which is the classic greedy for maximum non-overlapping intervals. Sorting by start could keep a long early interval that blocks many short ones, e.g. `[1,100]` before `[2,3],[4,5]`. Minimum removals equals total minus maximum kept.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) for the sort.
Space: O(1) extra (the sort is in place).

435.takeaway: Interval scheduling greedy: sort by end time, keep every interval that starts at or after the last kept end.

p: BST `[5,3,6,2,4,null,7]` (`5(3(2,4),6(,7))` in `v(left,right)` form), delete 3:

bullets: Result: `5(4(2,),6(,7))`. Node 3 now holds 4 and the old 4 was removed.

p: The in-order successor is the smallest value larger than the deleted node: larger than everything in its left subtree and no larger than anything else in its right subtree, so the BST order holds with no restructuring. The in-order predecessor (largest in the left subtree) works equally well.

bullets: Time: O(h): one search plus one walk down.

450.takeaway: BST deletion: 0 or 1 child → splice out; 2 children → copy the in-order successor's value and delete that node instead.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The total the array would have if every element equalled the minimum

p: Adding 1 to n−1 elements is the same, relatively, as subtracting 1 from one element. So each move can lower the gap of exactly one element toward the others. The elements end up equal when every element has come down to the minimum, which costs `nums[i] − min` moves for element i. Summing gives `sum − n·min`. The minimum never needs to be lowered.

453.takeaway: Increment n−1 elements ≡ decrement one element, so the answer is sum − n·min.

Reach for it when
rows: Scans right to left, so x plays the role of the '1' (smallest, leftmost)
Monotonic stack of candidate '3's: decreasing from bottom to top
The best '2' found so far: the largest value that was popped because a bigger value (the '3') came before it
x is a '1' smaller than the '2', and a '3' bigger than the '2' exists to its right → 132 found
while st and st[-1] < x: third = st.pop()
x is larger than the stack top; the popped value becomes the '2' and x the '3'

p: `[3,1,4,2]` scanned from the right:

Going right to left, when a value is popped by a larger one, the larger one is the '3' and the popped one is the '2'. Both are to the right of any future x. We only need to know the biggest valid '2', because any x below it makes a '1'. Scanning left to right would need to guess '1' candidates first.

bullets: Time: O(n): each value is pushed and popped at most once.

456.takeaway: 132 pattern: scan from the right with a decreasing stack; the last value popped is the best '2', and any smaller x completes the pattern.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Net balance per person: negative = owes money, positive = is owed
Reduce a transaction graph to net balances
debts = [v for v in bal.values() if v]
Keeps only people who are not already settled
Settles person i by transferring their whole balance to some later person, then recurses on i + 1
Backtracking over who settles with whom
Only pair a debtor with a creditor (opposite signs)
Tries each distinct balance value only once at this level
Apply the transfer, recurse, then undo it

p: `[[0,1,10],[2,0,5]]`: person 0 pays person 1 ten, person 2 pays person 0 five. Net balances: person 0 owes 5 (−5), person 1 is owed 10, person 2 owes 5 (−5), so `debts = [-5, 10, -5]`.
bullets: Two transfers settle everything (person 0 → 1 and person 2 → 1), so the answer is `2`.

blocks.h: Why can one person settle with a single transfer in the search?
p: Person i is fixed to settle completely, by sending or receiving their whole balance in exactly one transaction with some later person. That one transfer may leave the other person with a new balance, but person i is finished and is skipped from then on. The search chooses who that partner is, and the minimum over all partner choices is the answer. Skipping repeated balance values (`seen`) avoids exploring equivalent partners twice.

bullets: Time: exponential in the number of non-zero balances, about O((n−1)!) in the worst case; fine for the problem's small n (≤ 12 transactions).
Space: O(n) recursion plus the balances.

465.takeaway: Reduce to net balances, then backtrack: settle one person at a time with a person of opposite sign, undoing each trial.
